data.raw_text:
Typhoon Fung-Wong, locally known as Uwan in the Philippines, is the 26th named storm of the 2025 Pacific typhoon season and a rapidly intensifying tropical cyclone currently barreling across the Philippine Sea. It formed earlier this week and was officially upgraded to typhoon status by weather agencies on Friday evening, just hours after the previous storm, Typhoon Kalmaegi, was downgraded.
Current Status and Intensity
As of Saturday morning (November 8, 2025), Fung-Wong has sustained winds of 140 km/h (87 mph) with gusts reaching up to 170 km/h (106 mph). Its massive circulation spans approximately 1,500 km (932 miles) in diameter—large enough to blanket nearly the entire Philippines with rain and wind. Forecasters from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center and the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) predict it could escalate to super typhoon strength (winds of at least 185 km/h or 115 mph) before landfall.
Path and Forecast
The typhoon is moving westward toward the eastern coast of the Philippines and is expected to make landfall on Sunday (November 9), potentially near Legazpi City in the Bicol Region. After crossing Luzon, it may continue into the South China Sea, affecting southern Vietnam later in the week. Its expansive size means impacts could extend across Luzon (including Manila), the Visayas islands, and even as far as Siargao in the east.
Expected Impacts and Warnings
Fung-Wong poses significant threats of violent winds, life-threatening storm surges (up to 3-5 meters in coastal areas), and heavy rainfall leading to widespread flooding and landslides. Low-lying and coastal communities are at highest risk, with PAGASA urging immediate evacuations to higher ground. Several airlines, including Philippine Airlines, have already canceled flights, and all marine activities have been suspended nationwide. The storm's arrival comes amid recovery efforts from recent disasters, exacerbating vulnerabilities in infrastructure and emergency response.
Broader Context
This is the second major typhoon to strike the Philippines in less than a week, following the deadly Typhoon Kalmaegi (local name: Kristine), which killed nearly 200 people in the central Philippines—primarily from drowning in Cebu province—and five more in Vietnam. Kalmaegi's impacts were worsened by clogged waterways and delays in early warnings, displacing tens of thousands. Fung-Wong marks the 21st named storm to affect the country this year, highlighting the Philippines' position in the typhoon belt and the increasing intensity of storms linked to climate change.
For real-time updates, track it via official sources like PAGASA or the Joint Typhoon Warning Center. If you're in the affected areas, prioritize safety and follow local evacuation orders.
